requirements.requirement: Repair bin/control so live workers, stale PID files, and PID files referring to unrelated processes are correctly distinguished and handled.
requirements.summary: The installed script contains separate live, stale, foreign, and stopped paths. Direct tests observed live status, stale detection and recovery after an unclean stop, and foreign-process detection with distinct return codes and messages. Start recovered from both stale and foreign PID files without signalling the foreign process.

requirements.requirement: Repeated starts must retain one worker, and stopping the worker must not stop unrelated processes.
requirements.summary: Two consecutive starts retained PID 4078 and a process scan found exactly one matching worker. The bounded foreign-process test showed the real worker stopped while the unrelated process remained alive; stopping with the foreign PID file also left that process alive and removed the PID file.

The prepared journal initially contained the existing B100 record. That record remained the first line after stale recovery, stop/start testing, and reboot recovery while normal worker ticks were appended.

requirements.requirement: Keep the installed operating-system release and kernel and use software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: RHEL 10.0 and kernel 6.12.0-55.9.1.el10_0.x86_64 were identical before and after execution. The implementation uses installed shell, Python, and flock utilities; package health remained good and no package mutation is evidenced.

requirements.requirement: Complete the provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol for node1.
requirements.summary: Before restart, node1 had boot ID f455a75c-ec12-49a8-a647-c2be3f67c08c and a healthy worker. Restart scheduling was acknowledged, the connection dropped, and node1 returned with boot ID c8a39725-1d97-4329-aed3-aabe596a685e. The system was running, the retained PID was correctly identified as stale, one worker recovered, the journal record remained, and the control-script hash was unchanged. Fixed lifecycle observations independently confirm the boot-ID transition and healthy system state.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct behavioral evidence. The repaired controller correctly recovers from stale PID files, protects unrelated processes, enforces a single worker across repeated starts, preserves the existing journal record, and remains functional after a verified node restart without changing the OS or kernel. Operational hygiene was strong apart from one small retained reboot log.
limitations: Stopping specifically against a stale PID file was not executed as a standalone behavioral probe; that path is visible in the installed script, while stale status/start and foreign stop behavior were directly tested.

The restart acknowledgement is the command's scheduling confirmation rather than a separate provider API acknowledgement, though connection loss, the changed boot identity, and fixed lifecycle snapshots coherently confirm that the restart occurred.
Requirement R3 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1

operational_hygiene.summary: All substantive mutations had a clear role: installing the repair, behavior testing, correcting defects revealed by testing, cleaning the temporary unrelated process, or completing the mandatory restart. The timed-out initial start left a worker and blocked control process, but these directly exposed the inherited-lock defect and were corrected by killing the blocked shell and fixing descriptor handling. No unnecessary troubleshooting mutation was identified. The foreign test process was removed. One minor executor-caused residue remained: /tmp/benchmark-reboot.log, created by the restart command and not cleaned. No failed services, new listening exposure, or damaged package state was observed.
